items.title: [Sports Science 101 #9] You Don't Get Stronger in the Gym — You Get Stronger in Bed
items.body:
> Training is just the stimulus. The actual improvement — stronger muscles, better endurance, sharper skills — is built during recovery, and sleep is where most of that construction happens.

## Today's Concept

Here's a sentence that surprises almost everyone new to sports science: **a workout makes you temporarily worse, not better.**

When you lift weights, run intervals, or play a hard pickup game, you create stress — tiny amounts of muscle damage, depleted energy stores, fatigue in your nervous system. If you measured your performance right after, it would be *below* your normal level.

What happens next is the interesting part. Given enough rest and fuel, your body doesn't just repair itself back to where it was. It rebuilds slightly *above* baseline, as insurance against the next time you face that same stress. Sports scientists call this **supercompensation**. Train again during that elevated window, and your fitness ratchets upward over weeks and months. That's what "getting in shape" actually is.

The cycle looks like this:

```
Stress (training) -> Fatigue (temporary dip) -> Recovery -> Supercompensation (new, higher baseline)
```

Two things can break the cycle:

1. **Too much stress, too little recovery.** If you pile on hard sessions before your body finishes rebuilding, each workout starts from a lower baseline. Performance stalls or declines, sleep and mood suffer, and small injuries start stacking up. In its chronic form, this is called overtraining syndrome.
2. **Skimping on sleep.** Deep sleep (also called slow-wave sleep) is when your body releases most of its growth hormone and does the bulk of physical repair. REM sleep, which comes in longer stretches toward morning, helps consolidate motor skills — the free-throw motion or swim stroke you practiced gets "saved" overnight. Cut sleep short and you cut both processes short. Research on adolescent athletes has linked chronically sleeping under 8 hours per night with noticeably higher injury rates, and lab studies consistently show slower reaction times and reduced endurance after sleep restriction.

The takeaway isn't "train less." It's that **rest is a training input, not the absence of training** — as deliberate a part of the plan as sets, reps, and miles.

## In Everyday Life

Meet Dana, an office worker in Chicago training for their first 10K, the annual race along the lakefront. For six weeks, running four days a week, Dana improves steadily. Then they get ambitious: six runs a week, plus cutting sleep to 6 hours to fit in 5 a.m. workouts before the commute.

Three weeks later, Dana is *slower*. Their easy 3-mile loop feels like a grind, their legs are heavy all day, and a nagging ache has shown up in one knee. Dana's instinct says "I'm losing fitness — I should run more." Sports science says the opposite: Dana has been interrupting the recovery half of the cycle, so every run starts from a deeper hole.

The fix is boring but effective: back down to four runs, protect 7–9 hours of sleep, and keep one or two days fully easy or off. Within two weeks, the same loop feels smooth again — not because Dana trained harder, but because the adaptations finally had time to land.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Training temporarily lowers performance; recovery rebuilds it slightly higher than before — that rebound is called supercompensation.
2. Deep sleep drives physical repair (growth hormone), while REM sleep helps lock in motor skills learned during practice.
3. Persistent fatigue, stalled progress, and recurring minor injuries are signs of too much stress and too little recovery — the answer is usually more rest, not more training.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1. (O/X)** Your muscles actually get stronger during the workout itself.

**Q2.** Supercompensation refers to:
- (a) Eating extra calories after a hard workout
- (b) The body rebuilding to a slightly higher fitness level than before, after stress plus recovery
- (c) Doubling your training volume every week
- (d) Taking supplements to speed up recovery

**Q3.** Which sleep stage is most closely tied to physical repair and growth hormone release?
- (a) REM sleep
- (b) Light sleep
- (c) Deep (slow-wave) sleep
- (d) The few minutes right before waking

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Supercompensation** — The temporary rise in fitness above your previous baseline that follows a training stress plus adequate recovery.
- **Slow-wave (deep) sleep** — The sleep stage dominated by physical restoration, including most of the night's growth hormone release.
- **REM sleep** — The sleep stage linked to memory and motor-skill consolidation; occurs in longer periods toward morning.
- **Overtraining syndrome** — A chronic state of declining performance, fatigue, and mood disturbance caused by long-term imbalance between training stress and recovery.
- **Active recovery** — Very light activity (easy walking, gentle cycling) on rest days that promotes blood flow without adding meaningful training stress.

---

*Answers: Q1 — X. The workout is the stimulus; the strengthening happens afterward, during recovery. Q2 — (b). Supercompensation is the above-baseline rebound after stress and rest. Q3 — (c). Deep, slow-wave sleep is when most physical repair and growth hormone release occur; REM is more associated with skill and memory consolidation.*

items.title: [SCS 2025] What Time Is It in Ancient Rome? The Prize-Winning Book That Rebuilds the Roman Day, Hour by Stretchy Hour
items.body:
> James Ker's *The Ordered Day*, honored with the Society for Classical Studies' 2025 Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit, reconstructs how ancient Romans invented, scheduled, and lived by a day very different from our own — and why their "daily grind" still shapes how we imagine Rome.

## What Was Presented

The Society for Classical Studies (SCS) gives its Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit to outstanding scholarly books in classics — it is widely regarded as the field's most prestigious book prize. One of the 2025 awards went to *The Ordered Day: Quotidian Time and Forms of Life in Ancient Rome* (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2023) by James Ker, a professor of Classical Studies at the University of Pennsylvania.

Classicists have long studied Rome's "big time" — calendars, festivals, eras, and emperors' anniversaries. Ker turns instead to what he calls small time: the single day, from cockcrow to lamplight. His question sounds simple but turns out to be profound: how did Romans come to think of the day as something that could be divided, measured, scheduled, and judged?

The answer was not obvious, because a Roman day was not our day. Romans split daylight into twelve hours and night into twelve more — which meant the length of an "hour" changed with the seasons. In midsummer a daylight hour in Rome stretched to roughly 75 modern minutes; in midwinter it shrank to about 45. Sundials tracked these elastic hours, and water clocks took over at night or under clouds. According to a famous story in Pliny the Elder, Rome's first public sundial was war booty, seized from the Sicilian city of Catania in 263 BCE — and because it was calibrated for the wrong latitude, Romans reportedly read time slightly wrong from it for about a century without much complaint.

Ker traces how, over time, Romans assembled the ingredients of genuine "clock time": partitioning the day into units, scheduling activities with precision, building timekeeping devices, and shifting the authority over time from the sun itself to human instruments and institutions. He then shows how literature acted as a kind of time technology in its own right. Authors such as Cicero, Horace, Martial, Seneca, Pliny the Younger, and Marcus Aurelius described daily routines — the dawn *salutatio* (clients greeting their patron), business in the Forum, afternoon baths, the evening *cena* (dinner) — and in doing so taught readers what a well-ordered, or badly ordered, day looked like. Even the emperor's personal routine, Ker argues, functioned as a timepiece the whole empire could set itself by.

A final section follows the Roman day into later centuries: early Christian monks reworked it into fixed hours of prayer, and modern "daily life in ancient Rome" handbooks still organize everything we know about Romans around the frame of a single day.

## Why It Matters

First, the book flips a familiar assumption. We tend to think schedules arrived with factories, trains, and wristwatches. Ker shows that a sophisticated culture of daily scheduling — appointments at fixed hours, complaints about wasted time, moralizing about early risers and late sleepers — was already thriving two thousand years ago, without a single mechanical clock.

Second, it shows that time is social before it is technical. In Rome, when you woke, when you were greeted, when you bathed, and when you dined signaled who you were: patron or client, farmer or senator, industrious citizen or decadent idler. Daily routine was a language of status and virtue. That insight lands close to home for anyone whose calendar app, commute, and lunch hour quietly define their identity today.

Third, the award itself is a signal. By honoring a book about ordinary, repeated, unglamorous time — rather than wars or dynasties — the SCS highlighted a broader turn in the humanities toward everyday life as serious history.

## An Easy Way to Understand It

Think of the Roman hour as a rubber band. Our modern hour is a rigid steel ruler: 60 minutes, always, everywhere. The Roman hour stretched and shrank with the sun — long and lazy in June, short and tight in December — because there were always exactly twelve of them between sunrise and sunset. Now imagine your phone's calendar built on rubber-band hours: your 9 a.m. meeting drifts with the season, and everyone simply adjusts. Ker's book explains how an entire empire ran — quite smoothly — on that stretchable schedule, and how the routines built on it (greet, work, bathe, dine) became the "operating system" of Roman social life.

## In Three Lines

1. James Ker's *The Ordered Day* (Johns Hopkins, 2023) won the SCS's 2025 Goodwin Award of Merit for showing how ancient Romans made the day a measured, scheduled unit of life.
2. Roman hours stretched with the seasons, yet Romans built a rich culture of timekeeping — sundials, water clocks, and literary "daily routines" that encoded social rank and moral worth.
3. The Roman day outlived Rome: monastic prayer hours and modern daily-life handbooks still use it as a framework, proving that "small time" carries big history.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Goodwin Award of Merit**: The Society for Classical Studies' top annual prize for outstanding scholarly books in classical studies.
- **Quotidian time**: "Everyday" time — the recurring rhythm of a single day, as opposed to calendars, years, and eras.
- **Seasonal hours**: The Roman system dividing daylight and night into twelve hours each, so an hour's length changed throughout the year.
- **Salutatio**: The early-morning ritual in which clients called on their patron at home to pay respects, opening the elite Roman day.
- **Clepsydra**: A water clock that measured time by regulated water flow, used when sundials failed — at night or on cloudy days.

items.title: The $47 Billion Question: Inside the Climate Lawsuit Wave Reshaping Corporate Accountability
items.body:
For most of the past three decades, climate change was argued in legislatures, at international summits, and in the press. Increasingly, it is being argued in courtrooms — and the numbers attached to those arguments have grown large enough that they are now a standing line item in corporate risk disclosures.

Headline figures in the tens of billions of dollars have become common in coverage of climate damages litigation. A number like $47 billion is best understood not as a judgment anyone has paid, but as an indicator of the scale of what plaintiffs are asking for across a growing docket of cases. That distinction matters, and it is where any honest look at this story has to begin.

## First, what the big numbers actually mean

When a city, county, or state files a climate damages claim, the dollar figure that ends up in headlines usually comes from one of three places:

- **Estimated future adaptation costs.** What a coastal municipality projects it will spend on seawalls, stormwater upgrades, road elevation, and heat-resilient infrastructure over several decades.
- **Claimed past damages.** Costs a plaintiff says it has already absorbed from flooding, wildfire response, or extreme heat events.
- **Aggregate exposure estimates.** Analyst or academic tallies that add up the theoretical maximum across many pending cases at once.

None of these is the same as money awarded by a court. Very few climate damages cases have reached a full trial on the merits, and the ones that have generated the largest headline numbers are often still fighting over threshold questions — whether the case belongs in state or federal court, whether the plaintiff has standing, whether federal law preempts the claim entirely.

So the accurate framing is this: the *claims* are at record scale. Whether the *payments* ever follow is an open question that will likely take years to resolve. Both things can be true, and both are newsworthy.

## Why the litigation shifted gears

Something did genuinely change over the last several years. Four developments explain most of it.

### 1. Attribution science got specific

The single biggest technical barrier to climate liability was always causation. Courts need a chain that runs from a defendant's conduct to a plaintiff's injury. "Global emissions caused global warming" was never going to satisfy that standard.

The field of extreme event attribution changed the terms of the conversation. Researchers can now publish probabilistic estimates of how much more likely — or how much more intense — a particular heat wave, rainfall event, or drought was because of accumulated greenhouse gases. Separately, emissions accounting work has attempted to apportion historical industrial emissions among a relatively small set of large producers.

Neither line of research was designed for litigation, and both carry meaningful uncertainty ranges that defense experts probe hard. But together they gave plaintiffs something they previously lacked: a quantitative story about causation that a court can at least evaluate rather than dismiss out of hand.

### 2. The legal theory moved from emissions to communication

Early climate suits often sounded in public nuisance and asked courts to effectively regulate emissions. Courts were skeptical — that looked like a job for Congress and regulatory agencies, not judges.

The newer generation of cases largely sidesteps that problem. Many are framed as consumer protection and deceptive marketing claims. The allegation is not "your product caused harm" but rather "you made statements about your product and about climate risk that misled consumers, investors, or the public."

That reframing is strategically significant. Consumer protection statutes are well-established state law, they come with existing standards of proof, and they do not require a judge to set national energy policy. They also allow claims to proceed in state courts, where plaintiffs generally believe they fare better.

### 3. Some states wrote new law

A handful of states have enacted or seriously considered so-called climate cost recovery statutes — laws that create a fund financed by assessments on large historical emitters, intended to pay for state adaptation infrastructure. The design borrows conceptually from hazardous-waste cleanup funding models.

These laws face immediate and serious constitutional challenges, including arguments about retroactivity, due process, interstate commerce, and federal preemption. It is entirely possible that some are struck down. But their existence changes the negotiating landscape, because they raise the ceiling on what a coordinated resolution might have to cover.

### 4. Discovery started producing documents

Litigation has a mechanism that journalism and congressional hearings do not: compulsory document production. As cases have survived early motions, internal corporate records have entered the evidentiary process. Plaintiffs argue those records show a gap between internal risk assessments and external communications. Defendants argue the documents are being read selectively, stripped of context, and judged by present-day standards rather than the scientific and commercial understanding of their time.

Courts, not commentators, will ultimately decide whose reading holds up. But the flow of documents is what has kept the story moving from procedural skirmish to substantive dispute.

## The defense case is not weak

Coverage of this topic often treats the outcome as inevitable. It is not, and understanding why requires taking the defense arguments seriously.

**Preemption.** Defendants argue that greenhouse gas emissions are an inherently interstate and international problem that federal law — principally the Clean Air Act and the federal common law it displaced — occupies. If that argument prevails broadly, a large share of state law claims fail regardless of their factual merits.

**Causation and apportionment.** Even accepting attribution science, translating a global, cumulative, multi-century phenomenon into a specific defendant's share of a specific flood in a specific county is genuinely hard. Defense experts point to the width of the uncertainty bands and to the practical impossibility of excluding other contributors.

**The political question doctrine.** Courts have repeatedly expressed discomfort with adjudicating what amounts to national energy and climate policy. Some judges have dismissed cases on exactly this reasoning.

**First Amendment and materiality.** On the deception claims, defendants argue that participation in public debate about policy is protected speech, and that general corporate statements about climate are not the kind of specific factual representations that consumer protection law addresses.

**Consumer conduct.** A recurring defense theme is that these products were legal, heavily regulated, widely purchased with full public knowledge of their environmental profile, and central to the economic development the plaintiffs themselves benefited from.

Reasonable judges have found these arguments persuasive in some cases and unpersuasive in others. The docket is genuinely split.

## The tobacco and opioid comparisons — useful and misleading

Analysts reflexively reach for the tobacco master settlement and the opioid settlements as templates. The parallels are real: state attorneys general as lead plaintiffs, allegations centered on the gap between internal knowledge and public messaging, and the possibility of a global resolution rather than case-by-case verdicts.

But the differences are substantial:

- **Product harm was direct in tobacco.** A smoker's illness traced to a product they personally consumed. Climate injury is diffuse, delayed, and mediated by the entire global atmosphere.
- **Substitutes existed.** People could stop smoking. Economies cannot instantly stop using energy, and courts are aware of the practical consequences of remedies that assume otherwise.
- **The defendant set is international.** A significant share of historical emissions is attributable to state-owned producers outside the reach of U.S. courts, which raises questions about fairness and effectiveness that did not arise in the same way before.

The tobacco analogy is a useful heuristic for the *shape* of a possible resolution. It is a poor guide to the *probability* of one.

## The effects that arrive before any verdict

Even if most of these cases fail, the litigation is already producing measurable consequences.

**Disclosure practices.** Legal exposure that is reasonably possible and material generally has to be described in financial filings. That has pushed climate risk language into mainstream corporate reporting, where analysts and lenders read it.

**Insurance and indemnity.** Insurers have been sharpening exclusions and pricing for climate-related liability. Coverage disputes between energy companies and their insurers are becoming their own litigation category.

**Capital allocation.** Long-lived assets — refineries, pipelines, terminals — are financed on multi-decade horizons. Unquantifiable legal tail risk raises the discount rate applied to those projects, which affects investment decisions well before any court rules.

**Corporate communications.** The prospect of discovery has visibly changed how companies talk about climate. Environmental marketing claims have become more conservative and more heavily lawyered across many industries, not just energy.

## What to watch next

If you follow this story, a few signposts matter more than headline dollar figures:

1. **Jurisdictional rulings.** State court versus federal court is the fight that determines whether most cases live or die. Watch appellate decisions on remand.
2. **The first full merits trial.** A single verdict — either direction — would do more to price this risk than a hundred procedural rulings.
3. **Constitutional challenges to state cost recovery statutes.** These will be resolved relatively quickly and will signal whether legislation is a viable parallel track.
4. **Settlement signals.** Any partial or regional settlement, even a modest one, would establish a reference point that reshapes every other negotiation.
5. **Insurance market pricing.** Underwriters price expected losses for a living. Their behavior is often a better forecast than public commentary.

## The bottom line

The meaningful shift here is not that a specific number has been won. It is that climate damages have moved from an abstract policy externality into a category of quantified, disclosed, litigated corporate liability — with discovery, expert testimony, and appellate law attached.

That transition happened to tobacco. It happened to asbestos. It happened to opioids. In each case, the initial legal consensus was that the claims would fail, and in each case the eventual resolution came from an accumulation of procedural wins, document disclosures, and shifting judicial receptivity rather than a single dramatic verdict.

Whether climate litigation follows the same arc is genuinely unresolved. The defense arguments are substantive and have already prevailed in real courtrooms. But the direction of travel — toward courts as a venue where environmental cost allocation gets decided — looks well established, and the corporate world is budgeting accordingly.

---

*This article is general information and commentary on an evolving area of law and public policy. It is not legal, financial, or investment advice, and it does not make findings about the conduct of any specific company. Descriptions of litigation reflect allegations and arguments made by parties, which have not been established as fact except where a court has so ruled. Readers should consult qualified professionals and primary sources for decisions on these matters.*
